legal: None for this recommendation. Separate court cases over VOA cuts are described in ch08-013.

happened: On March 14, 2025, President Trump ordered USAGM, which runs Voice of America, cut to the minimum the law requires. Most VOA staff were put on leave and about 85% of USAGM jobs were eliminated by mid-2025. Congress did not abolish the agency; it funded USAGM at about $653 million for fiscal 2026, about 25% less than the year before.

key_dates.event: Executive Order 14238 orders USAGM reduced to the legal minimum.
Federal judge orders VOA restored (preliminary injunction).
Fiscal 2026 spending law funds USAGM at $652.7 million.
Judge rules acting CEO Kari Lake served unlawfully and voids her actions, including layoffs.

legal: In the U.S. District Court for D.C., Judge Royce Lamberth issued a preliminary injunction in April 2025; the D.C. Circuit stayed parts of it in May 2025. On March 7, 2026, he ruled Kari Lake's leadership violated the Vacancies Act and voided her actions, and on March 17 ordered over 1,000 VOA employees back to work. The government appealed, and in March 2026 a D.C. Circuit panel paused the return-to-work order while the appeal goes forward.
closeness: Partial match. The administration moved to dismantle USAGM, close to "defund and disestablish," but Congress kept the agency and most of its funding, and courts reversed key steps.
uncertain: The D.C. Circuit had not ruled on the merits of the appeal as of the newest reports found; employees were to stay on paid leave meanwhile. Newest source: July 2026 (CRS).

happened: In July 2025, Congress passed and President Trump signed the Rescissions Act of 2025, which canceled about $1.1 billion already set aside for the Corporation for Public Broadcasting. CPB said it would close, and its board voted on January 5, 2026 to dissolve the organization.

key_dates.event: Executive Order 14290 orders an end to federal funding for NPR and PBS.
Rescissions Act of 2025 signed, canceling CPB funding.
CPB announces it will wind down.
CPB board votes to dissolve.

legal: NPR and PBS sued over Executive Order 14290. On March 31, 2026, Judge Randolph Moss of the U.S. District Court for D.C. ruled the order's funding cutoff violated the First Amendment and blocked it, with a partial final judgment on April 23, 2026; the remaining claims were dismissed and the case closed on July 17, 2026. That ruling concerns the executive order, not the law passed by Congress.
closeness: Same goal and mechanism: Congress ended federal funding for CPB. It was done through a rescissions bill rather than the President refusing to sign a spending bill.
uncertain: The White House suggested it would appeal, but no appeal was found in case records reviewed in October 2026. Whether any future funding could be restored is not known. Newest source: July 2026.

happened: On March 15, 2025, the U.S. Agency for Global Media (USAGM) ended its grant to the Open Technology Fund, a nonprofit that pays for tools to get around internet censorship. The fund sued. On March 26, 2026, a federal judge ruled the termination unlawful and said the fund must receive the $43.5 million that Congress set aside for it.

key_dates.event: USAGM ends the Open Technology Fund's grant.
Federal judge rules the termination unlawful.

legal: Judge Royce Lamberth of the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia granted the fund summary judgment (a final ruling) on March 26, 2026, finding the termination violated the Administrative Procedure Act. An earlier preliminary injunction order is also reported. No appeal ruling was found.
closeness: The chapter wanted the fund's work and money moved back to an in-house USAGM Office of Internet Freedom that the agency and Congress could oversee. USAGM instead tried to cut off the fund, and a court stopped that. No rebuilt in-house office was found.
uncertain: Whether USAGM revived its Office of Internet Freedom, whether the money has been paid, and whether the ruling was appealed are not known. Newest source: March 2026.

happened: After the March 2025 order to shrink USAGM, the agency was run by acting leaders while no chief executive was confirmed. Victor Morales served as acting CEO, and Kari Lake, first named senior adviser, later acted as CEO. On March 7, 2026, a federal judge ruled Lake had no lawful authority to serve as acting CEO and voided her actions, including August 2025 layoff notices to 532 workers.

key_dates.event: Order to cut USAGM to its legal minimum; acting leaders run the agency.
Judge rules Lake's service as acting CEO unlawful and voids her actions.

legal: Judge Royce Lamberth of the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia granted summary judgment to employees and their union, finding Lake's role violated the Federal Vacancies Reform Act and the Appointments Clause. Lake said she would appeal; no appeal ruling was found.
closeness: The chapter wanted strong acting leaders in place while a CEO nominee awaited Senate confirmation. Acting leaders were installed, but a court ruled that the main one was not lawfully serving.
uncertain: Whether a CEO has been nominated or confirmed, and the appeal's status, are not known. Newest source: March 2026.
